nameStory: Large Thyme gets its name from its relatively broad leaves compared to other thyme species - hence its alternate name "broad-leaved thyme." The word "thyme" comes from the Greek word "thymos," meaning courage, as ancient warriors believed the herb would give them bravery in battle. Despite being called "large," this little plant still only grows about as tall as a ruler!
description: Large Thyme is a low-growing, spreading mini-shrub that forms fragrant carpets across the ground. This aromatic little plant reaches only 2-10 inches tall but can spread up to 10 inches wide, creating dense mats of tiny, oval leaves. In early summer, it produces clusters of small lilac-pink flowers that buzz with pollinator activity. The entire plant releases a strong, pleasant herbal scent when brushed against or crushed.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs along square stems - crush them between your fingers for an intense, spicy-sweet thyme fragrance that's unmistakable

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny lilac-pink flowers clustered at stem tips in early summer, each flower less than a quarter-inch long with a tubular shape typical of the mint family

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats that hug the ground, with woody stems at the base that feel slightly rough and branched

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Square stems that feel distinctly four-angled when rolled between your fingers - a telltale sign of the mint family

habitat: Large Thyme thrives in sunny, well-drained areas with sandy or rocky soils, often found in disturbed sites like old fields, roadsides, and garden edges. In New England, look for it in areas that stay relatively dry, as it doesn't tolerate soggy conditions. It's commonly found as an escape from cultivation, spreading from herb gardens into nearby wild spaces.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small, fresh green leaves on woody stems. The plant begins to spread and fill out from its winter dormancy.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering time in early summer with lilac-pink blooms attracting bees and butterflies. Leaves are at their most aromatic during warm, dry weather.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and leaves may take on slightly purplish tints. The plant remains green and aromatic well into autumn.
seasonality.winter: Becomes semi-dormant with reduced foliage, but the woody stems and some leaves often persist through mild New England winters.

funFact: Large Thyme is so aromatic that medieval people believed its scent could give them prophetic dreams - they would place sprigs under their pillows hoping to see the future while they slept!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Mother of Thyme, but Large Thyme has broader, more oval leaves (Mother of Thyme's are narrower and more needle-like) and tends to grow in a more upright manner rather than completely flat against the ground.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this European native with our native wild mints - while they're in the same family, true thymes have that distinctive Mediterranean herb garden smell that's much more concentrated and spicy than typical wild mints.
compareHints: Compared to its relative Mother of Thyme, Large Thyme has broader, more egg-shaped leaves and grows more upright rather than completely prostrate. Mother of Thyme forms flatter mats and has much narrower, almost linear leaves that feel more needle-like to the touch. Both share the classic thyme fragrance, but Large Thyme's scent tends to be slightly more lemony.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Mother of Thyme differs from Large Thyme (its closest New England relative) by its much more prostrate, mat-forming growth habit and earlier blooming time.
